<reason>CON won by disciplining the whole debate around one concrete test case (the dam) and forcing PRO into a dilemma it never fully escaped: either the "clearly excessive" balancing does real work and is an unpredictable policy verdict with prison attached, or PRO's fallback (a rejected equally-cheap alternative with no material benefit) collapses into conduct already criminal as abuse of office. PRO's answers were competent and honestly formatted (A1/A2), and its closing point that a complicit host's refusal to prosecute domestic corruption is exactly why a backstop matters was a fair partial reply, but PRO never supplied the stable standard CON demanded and largely reasserted rather than resolved. On jurisdiction, CON's point that the mechanism fails precisely where PRO says it is needed (complicit host must surrender its own minister) landed harder than PRO's travel-arrest scenario, which CON deflated with the ordinary observation that indicted heads of state have flown home from member states. CON's answer to PRO's recklessness question (conduct against a standard of care vs. weighing whether the outcome was worth it) was adequate and PRO didn't press it further. CON carried real execution costs—two clipped turns and nonexistent reference IDs [P1.3, P2.3]—which keeps the margin competitive rather than solid, but CON made the decisive clash clearer and easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B4.2]–[B4.3] and [B5.2]–[B5.3]: after PRO answered the "what fact proves clearly excessive" question with the rejected-alternative scenario, CON argued PRO had abandoned the balancing element—making the crime either arbitrary (real trade-offs) or redundant (destruction for no reason). PRO's closing reply about non-prosecuting hosts only partly blunted this.</best_rebuttal>
